title: How people take a lie
translation: Someone who truly understands people never gets them wrong, not in the slightest.

Say someone makes up a story and passes it round to fool people. Some people believe it straight away and are taken in, exactly as planned. Some believe it so completely that they add their own bits and make it even more of a tangle. Some don't think anything of it and pay no attention. Some aren't quite sure and keep turning it over, half believing it and half not. Some don't really think it's true, but somebody said it, so it's probably so, and they leave it at that. Some nod wisely and smile as if they'd worked it all out, and have no idea at all. Some guess what's going on and think, "Ah, so that's it," but still wonder if they might be wrong. Some clap their hands and laugh: "So that's all it was!" Some see through it but say nothing, and since they're sure, they don't make a fuss and carry on just like the people who know nothing. And some understand from the start what the story is for, aren't fooled for a moment, and join in to help the person who made it up.

Even with a joke among fools, someone who knows can read every one of these reactions in people's words and faces. So someone who sees clearly looks at confused people like us as easily as at something in the palm of his hand.
But this kind of guesswork is no way to measure the Buddha's teaching.

literal: The eye with which a person of understanding sees people surely has not the slightest point of error.
For example, when a certain person makes up a lie in the world and deceives people, there are people who honestly think it true and are deceived just as he says.
There are people who form too deep a belief and, still more troublesomely, add to the lie with their own understanding.
Also there are people who think nothing of it and pay no attention.
Also there are people who feel a little doubtful and, neither relying on it nor not relying on it, keep pondering.
Also there are people who, though they do not feel it to be true, since it is what people say, think 'it may be so' and leave it there.
Also there are people who, pretending to have guessed and understood in various ways, nod cleverly and sit smiling, but know nothing at all.
Also there are people who guess it out and, while thinking 'ah, it seems to be so', still doubt, (thinking) 'there may yet be a mistake'.
Also there are people who clap their hands and laugh: 'There was nothing special about it.'
Also there are people who understand but do not say they know, and those who are not in doubt pass without any fuss, in the same way as people who do not know.
Also there are people who understand the purpose of this lie from the beginning, are not deceived at all, become of one mind with the person who made it up, and join forces.
Even in a joke among fools, before a person who knows, these various characteristics will surely be known without concealment, whether in words or in faces.
Still more, an enlightened person's seeing us who are confused is like seeing a thing on the palm of the hand.
However, by this kind of guesswork one should not go so far as to compare and speak of the Buddhist Law.

notes.text: A false friend: {達人|たつじん} here is someone who understands the way things are, a wise person, as the 1925 edition explains. Modern {達人|たつじん} is a master of a skill, as in martial arts. {眼|まなこ}: 'eye', the edition's reading.
{虚言|そらごと}: 'a lie, a made-up story'. {構|かま}へ{出|いだ}す: to make something up on purpose. The rest of the section is one long list, each item starting with また or {又|また}, 'and also'.

notes.quote: なほ煩はしく虚言を心得添ふる
notes.text: {心得|こころえ}{添|そ}ふ: 'to add one's own understanding', so they make the lie bigger by explaining it. {煩|わづら}はし: 'troublesome, tangled'.

notes.quote: たのむにもあらずたのまずもあらで
notes.text: 'Neither relying on it nor not relying on it': caught in between.
つやつや + a negative: 'not at all'. These people act as if they understood the trick.
もこそ: a worry, 'there might be…'. They have guessed right but don't trust their own guess.

notes.quote: このさまざまの得たる所
notes.text: 'What each of them has grasped', which the 1925 edition explains as 'their particular character'. The wise observer sees which of the types each person is.
{掌|たなごころ}: the palm of the hand. Seeing something on your own palm: nothing could be clearer or closer.

notes.quote: 仏法までをなずらへ言ふべきにはあらず
notes.text: なずらふ (also spelt なぞらふ): 'to compare, to treat as the same'. Kenkō does not explain the sentence, and the translation does not either. Commentaries read it in two ways: the Buddha's teaching cannot be judged by such guesswork about people, or the teaching, which also uses made-up stories as a means to teach, must not be put on a level with lies.
